page.title: What to Wear on a Boat Trip in Marbella: Seasonal Packing Guide

data.meta_description: Wondering what to wear on a boat trip Marbella? Our seasonal packing guide covers sun protection, layers, footwear & more. Get ready to sail from Puerto Banús.
data.summary: A practical, season-by-season guide to dressing for a boat trip in Marbella, covering sun protection, layers, footwear, and what to bring for comfort and safety on the water.
key_facts: Seasonal layering: summer light, spring/autumn add a windproof layer.
Non-slip, white-soled shoes are essential on deck.
Sun protection: SPF 50+, sunglasses, and a wide-brim hat.
Evening trips: temperatures drop 5-8°C after sunset.
Bring a light jacket or fleece for breezy cruising.
Swimwear and a quick-dry towel for swim stops.
Avoid dark colours that absorb heat and show salt stains.
All our charters include towels, water, and soft drinks.

faq.q: What should I wear on a boat trip in Marbella in summer?
faq.a: In summer (June–September), wear light, breathable fabrics like cotton or linen. A swimsuit under your clothes is smart for swim stops. Pack a light cover-up or shirt for after swimming, and always bring a windproof layer — even at 30°C, sea breezes can feel cool when cruising at speed.

faq.q: Do I need special shoes for a boat?
faq.a: Yes. Non-slip, white-soled deck shoes or trainers are best. They grip wet surfaces and won't mark the deck. Avoid black-soled shoes, high heels, and flip-flops for walking on deck — they're slippery and unsafe. Keep flip-flops for the beach stops.

faq.q: What should I wear in spring or autumn on a Marbella boat trip?
faq.a: Spring (March–May) and autumn (October–November) are cooler. Wear layers: a long-sleeve top, a light jumper or fleece, and a windproof jacket. Temperatures on the water can be 5–8°C lower than on land, especially in the morning or late afternoon. Closed-toe shoes are a must.

faq.q: Can I wear jeans on a boat trip?
faq.a: Technically yes, but we don't recommend it. Jeans are heavy when wet, restrict movement, and can chafe when you're sitting for long periods. Choose quick-dry trousers, leggings, or shorts instead. If you do wear jeans, pick a relaxed fit and avoid them for swim-heavy trips.

faq.q: What should I bring for sun protection on a boat?
faq.a: Bring SPF 50+ sunscreen (water-resistant), a wide-brim hat, and polarised sunglasses. The sun reflects off the sea, so you burn faster on water. Reapply every two hours, especially after swimming. Our charters include water and soft drinks, but you should bring extra hydration.

faq.q: Is it cold on a boat at night in Marbella?
faq.a: Evening cruises can feel chilly once the sun sets. Temperatures drop noticeably, and the sea breeze adds to the chill. Bring a warm fleece, a windbreaker, or a light jacket. If you're doing a sunset charter, long trousers and closed shoes are more comfortable.

faq.q: What do I wear for a swim stop?
faq.a: Wear your swimsuit underneath your clothes — it's the easiest. Pack a quick-dry towel and a change of underwear. After swimming, put on a dry cover-up or rash guard to protect against sunburn. Our boats have fresh water showers to rinse off salt.

faq.q: Are there any clothing restrictions on our boats?
faq.a: We ask that you avoid black-soled shoes (they mark decks), high heels, and sharp objects that could damage upholstery. For safety, no loose scarves or dangling jewellery when the boat is moving. Otherwise, dress comfortably — casual resort wear is perfect.

data.body_html:
Packing for a boat trip in Marbella isn't about fashion — it's about comfort, safety, and being smart with the sun. The Mediterranean climate is forgiving, but the sea breeze, glare, and sudden temperature drops can catch you out. This seasonal guide tells you exactly what to wear, what to bring, and what to leave at home, so you can focus on the coastline from Puerto Banús to Cabopino.

Why dressing for the boat matters

On land, Marbella can hit 32°C in July. On the water, it can feel 5°C cooler when you're cruising at 20 knots. But the sun's reflection off the sea means you burn faster than you would on the beach. Add the wind, and you have a microclimate that demands layers and protection. The golden rule: dress in breathable layers you can remove or add as conditions change.

Summer (June – September): light and breezy

Summer is peak season for charters from Puerto Banús. Days are long, sea temperatures reach 24–26°C, and swim stops are a must. Here's your summer kit:

  • Swimsuit under your clothes — you'll want to jump in at Cala del Faro or Cala Cortés.
  • Light cotton or linen shirt and shorts — breathable, quick-drying.
  • A rash guard or cover-up for after swimming — protects against sunburn.
  • Wide-brim hat and polarised sunglasses — the glare off the sea is intense.
  • Non-slip deck shoes or trainers — white soles only, please.
  • A light windbreaker — even in August, the breeze at speed feels cool.

Spring & autumn (March – May, October – November): layers are your friend

Spring and autumn in Marbella are gorgeous, with air temperatures around 18–24°C. But the sea is still cool (16–20°C), and mornings can be crisp. For these shoulder seasons, pack:

  • A long-sleeve base layer — merino or synthetic, not cotton.
  • A light fleece or jumper — for when the wind picks up.
  • A waterproof windbreaker — essential for spray and sudden showers.
  • Long trousers or leggings — warmer than shorts, and they protect against sun.
  • Closed-toe, non-slip shoes — your feet will thank you.

Don't be fooled by the afternoon sun. On a 4-hour charter, temperatures can drop 8°C between noon and 4pm, especially in October.

Winter (December – February): crisp but sailable

Winter charters are less common but still possible. Expect 12–17°C on land, and 8–12°C on the water. If you're heading out on one of our larger yachts like the Ferretti 94 or Mangusta 80, you'll appreciate the enclosed saloon. Dress as if for a coastal walk:

  • Thermal base layers.
  • Warm fleece or softshell jacket.
  • Waterproof and windproof outer shell.
  • Warm hat and gloves — yes, even in Marbella.
  • Sturdy, non-slip boots or trainers.

Footwear: the unsung hero

Flip-flops are fine for the beach, but on a moving boat they're a hazard. The deck gets wet, and you need grip. Choose white-soled deck shoes, boat trainers, or even non-slip water shoes. Avoid black soles — they leave scuff marks that are hard to remove. If you're barefoot, be careful on hot deck surfaces; they can get uncomfortably warm in direct sun.

Sun protection: non-negotiable

Even on cloudy days, UV rays reflect off the water and can burn you within 20 minutes. Use SPF 50+ water-resistant sunscreen, and reapply every two hours — more if you're swimming. A wide-brim hat protects your face, neck, and ears. Polarised sunglasses reduce glare and help you spot marine life, like dolphins off the coast of Estepona.

What to bring beyond clothes

Our charters include water, soft drinks, beer, white wine, cava, light snacks, and towels. But you might want to add:

  • Extra water bottle — hydration is key in the sun.
  • Lip balm with SPF — wind and sun dry lips fast.
  • Motion sickness bands — if you're prone, take them before you board.
  • A dry bag for your phone and camera.
  • Change of underwear — you'll appreciate it after a swim.

Dressing for evening and sunset cruises

Sunset cruises from Puerto Banús are magical — the sky turns orange over La Concha. But once the sun dips, the temperature drops fast. Bring a warm layer even in summer. For evening charters on our Azimut 58 Flybridge, a light jacket and long trousers are comfortable. And if you're heading to a beach club after, a smart-casual outfit in a small bag works well.

What not to wear

Avoid the following to stay safe and keep our boats in top condition:

  • Black-soled shoes — they leave permanent marks.
  • High heels — dangerous on deck and damaging to upholstery.
  • Jewellery that dangles — can catch on lines and fittings.
  • Heavy cotton jeans — heavy and slow to dry if wet.
  • Loose scarves or long skirts — they flap in the wind and can trip you.

Final tips for a comfortable trip

Check the marine forecast before you head out — our skippers always do. Dress in layers you can adjust, and don't forget that the sea breeze can be deceptive. If you're unsure, ask our team when you book. And remember, every charter includes a licensed skipper, fuel, insurance, and IVA — so you just need to show up in the right gear. Ready to set sail?
